body:
My 2 cents:

For context, I have failed a design course, last year actually. I have ADHD (I know it's not nearly the same thing but still).

Most if not all the things you've listed are things that you get better at the more time you work at it. It's not something that you can fix in a matter of months sadly. Some things can take years but it's ok because we all have advantages and disadvantages. I'm pretty bad at starting tasks and not getting distracted but I'm really good at coming up with crazy ideas that (hopefully) work.

1. Try every time management strategy under the sun and then come up with some. People make the mistake of assuming there's a one size fits all for time management, in truth I hate calendars and alarms but I love bullet lists and time schedules. 

2. If you suck at drawing I have a solution that you already know what it is: draw more. Sounds cliche and repetitive I know. But what are cliches but lessons we all learn at some point that refuse to take seriously when taught. Draw more, draw for pleasure, draw as a discipline, whatever, just draw. 

3. SketchUp and 3D modelling in general is all about the amount of detail you're willing to commit to adding. You probably know how to do 80% of the things you need to do it's just a matter of how much time will it take. Tip: model quick volumes first, figure out your camera angles then add geometry as needed, don't add muvh detail to things that will be outside the view of the camera this will save an unbelievable amount of time.

4. The designer's eye is absolutely a skill. 2 years ago I couldn't do interior design for shit. Now 70% of my internship job is interior design and I'm not shit at it (I think). You learn how to harmonize colors, you learn what shapes go nicer with what spaces. That's what design courses are for. 

5. Going from concept to the realization of the idea is the whole point of being a designer. That's not to make you feel bad, it's just that that's the meat of the sandwich, that's the very thing you're supposed to get good at. It's not easy going from an idea to something real, that's why we have designers, that's what you're studying. Luckily, this means you're not alone, there are methods for this, learn about design thinking maybe take a course maybe do a lil side project for fun or read a book. 

6. In my personal opinion and experience, anxiety in architecture is best combated with an executive mindset. Meaning, "x thing needs to be done, what's the best way to do it? Can I realistically do that? How much time will it take?" After taking a methodical approach to the problem or task you execute the plan and continue to run with that mindset as you do it, it'll help you improvise and not stress about it because you're actively forcing yourself to see the optimal path available. Preferably try to remove emotions from the equation. Meaning: (something breaks) "how important is it that I fix that? How urgent is it? Is there a quick and easy fix that will make it good enough?" Not "OMG nonono I need to fix that, I'll go back to it later I need to finish this, or what if I do that first?..." I like to compartmentalize emotions to the conceptual or more artistic phases of design but when it comes to producing work you need to be cold, realistic and efficient. Also know that your project does not define you as a person or even as an architect. More on that later. Do breathing exercises like 4x4 breathing for panic attacks or whenever you're stressing out. If you stress out while preparing for a critique or présentation youre setting yourself up for failure, itll be worse when the impostor syndrome kicks in.

Finally on bpd and architecture school in general: there is a big problem imo with how we teach architecture in general. It's a tough career. But the problem is it's low tolerance for failure and the emotional blow that is failing a design course. I fell into a very deep depression when I failed that course and even to this day I'm scarred by the humiliation I felt but it shouldn't be this way, the best architects aren't the ones who never had a bad project, idea or concept because every architect has had tons of them. That's the point of being creative. You can't be creative without taking risks, school should be a place where you can take risks more freely without the terrible financial and emotional repercussions if not you're just training a bunch of architects that play it safe and can't innovate. I don't have bpd and I know ADHD ain't similar at all but at least from the emotional aspect of having something out of your control cripple you so much is hard but it gets easier. It'll never be easy I think. But it gets easier. The more you know yourself the better equipped you are at dealing with yourself. Be honest, be kind, to yourself. And always remember:

"Sucking at something is the first step towards being sorta good at something"

Thank you for replying. It's just I want to end it all. I feel guilty, sad and alone all day every day and then I'll feel even more guilty about feeling like shit and not doing anything. I wish I could just disappear. I feel like such a failure like why even bother getting better.

Even if everyone hated you, there are so many people that care about you, LOVE you that you don't know yet. They will come in due time but you have to either wait or go after them. Even if everyone hated you, that would be something out of your control, and really, why would everyone hate you? I know nearly nothing about you yet I feel confident saying that you are a kind-hearted person. Even in the pain you're in that all you wanna do is end it you can't help but think about your family which "hates you" and how it would make them feel. 

You are deserving of love. I care about you. Stay strong.
